item.content:encoded:
New York Yankees infielder Anthony Volpe is four games into his new role as a big-league second baseman after Jazz Chisholm Jr. landed on the injured list with a sprained right thumb. Volpe hasn't committed an error yet, and while the sample is tiny, the eye test feels so right. Volpe just looks comfortable out there.
His Jeter-esque jump throw on Sunday (from second base, but still!) was such a rewarding watch for Yankees fans who have experienced the dreadful lows of Volpe's up-and-down season and career. It looked and felt so much more iconic than it was.
It didn't take long for Anthony Volpe to learn second base for the Yankees
Volpe looking smooth at second is a bittersweet reality for Yankees fans, especially those with a quick trigger to criticize the team's development and roster decisions. On one hand, New York's decision to send Volpe down to the minors and learn second base this season has ... worked! On the other hand, this exact plan should have been put into motion a long time ago.
It's kind of like turning in your book report a month late in middle school. The teacher is like, "Well, thanks ... but I just remembered again that you never handed this in." You might've been better off just taking the zero and acing the next one.
If Volpe keeps acing second base — and sustains this level of defense into 2027 and beyond alongside George Lombard Jr. — the Yankees will have salvaged Volpe's career and somewhat made up for their entire mishandling of his development.
Then again, should the Yankees really get any credit for salvaging anything here, especially since it was the organization itself that contributed to this mess? Even now, it took an injury to Chisholm (not his horrid season and Volpe's red-hot bat in the minors) to give Volpe another opportunity. This decision was made for the Yankees, not by them. And it came way, way too late. On second thought, they don't get any credit here.
Anthony Volpe as a second-base solution should have been obvious to the Yankees years ago
Any player evaluator of worth should have been able to look at Volpe and surmise that a move from shortstop to second base made sense. Volpe won a Gold Glove as a rookie shortstop in 2023, but his range, arm, and consistency declined after that. Isn't that pretty much the precise recipe for a move from short to second, if you had to literally write the script?
The Yankees' problem with Volpe over the years, as has been acknowledged ad nauseam, is that they made "New York Yankees starting shortstop" Volpe's identity (rather than his job) and hugged that identity too tightly. It became a stranglehold that suffocated Volpe and had Aaron Boone and Brian Cashman at their most delusional in interviews, which is saying a lot.
The funny thing is that Volpe's never been against changing positions. He said unironically that he'd play catcher. It was Boone and Cashman who were stubborn, and they never actually lessened their grip on this situation. George Lombard Jr. undid that grip for them, and then Chisholm went down.
To the non-Yankee fan, the Yankees might look smart for putting Volpe at second base. But for the die-hards, this decision — and Volpe's good performance at second so far — hurts as much as it excites. At least for now.

item.title: [Pinstripes Nation] Lombard Se Lleva La Culpa, Pero La Derrota Por 5-4 De Los Yankees Ante Los Twins, Tras 13 Entradas, Tiene Muchos Culpables
item.dc:creator: Esteban Quiñones

item.content:encoded:
MINNEAPOLIS — Anthony Volpe bateó con tanta fuerza que perdió el equilibrio, convencido de que la pelota se había ido fuera. En cambio, rebotó contra el muro alto del centro-derecha, un doble de dos carreras que igualó el marcador para los Yankees con dos outs en la novena entrada. Durante un momento intenso y emocionante el miércoles, Nueva York parecía dispuesta a llevarse la barrida.
Lo que vino después fueron cuatro entradas más en las que el equipo llegaba hasta la puerta y se negaba a cruzarla. Los Yankees se pusieron por delante en la décima. Volvieron a hacerlo en la undécima. Llenaron las bases sin outs en la duodécima. Cada vez acababan con un empate o con una remontada desperdiciada.
Un viaje que debería haber acabado con una barrida acabó poniendo de manifiesto el único punto débil que un aspirante al título no puede permitirse arrastrar hasta octubre. No se trató de un colapso del bullpen ni de un rebote desafortunado. Fue la alineación de los Yankees la que no paraba de preparar la mesa, pero nunca se sentaba a comer.
La culpa final recayó en un novato que no se la merecía él solo.
Los Minnesota Twins vencieron a los Yankees por 5-4 en 13 entradas, poniendo fin a ese partido maratoniano con un sencillo de Victor Caratini en la primera base que rebotó en el montículo y se coló por debajo del guante de George Lombard Jr. en la segunda base. Con esta derrota, Nueva York queda con un balance de 88-64, a cuatro partidos de los Rays de Tampa Bay en la División Este de la Liga Americana, a falta de 10 partidos por disputar. Los Yankees ya tienen asegurada su plaza en los playoffs, pero el título de la división y la exención de la primera ronda se les están escapando.
Una remontada que no llevó a ninguna parte
Nueva York había sumado cuatro hits en ocho entradas y perdía por 2-0, mientras que el lanzador diestro de los Twins, Zebby Matthews, había ponchado a ocho. Entonces llegó la novena entrada. Lombard conectó un sencillo, Paul Goldschmidt le siguió y el corredor suplente José Caballero preparó el terreno para Volpe.
Volpe impulsó las dos carreras, lo que le supuso al cerrador de los Twins, Yoendrys Gómez, su primer salvamento fallido del año y obligó a jugar entradas extras.
Ali Sánchez impulsó al corredor automático con un sencillo en la décima entrada, dando a los Yankees su primera ventaja. Luke Keaschall respondió con un sencillo que empató el partido ante David Bednar. Un fly de sacrificio de Caballero puso a Nueva York por delante en la undécima. Royce Lewis igualó el marcador. Dos ventajas, dos respuestas inmediatas.
La entrada que dará que hablar
La 12.ª es la entrada que los aficionados volverán a ver una y otra vez. Los Yankees llenaron las bases sin outs, la situación que debería haber sentenciado el partido. Pero no sacaron nada de ella.
Heliot Ramos, que bateaba en el turno de Aaron Judge, mandó una bola corta hacia el montículo. Travis Adams la convirtió en una doble jugada 1-2-3. Sánchez se fue con un strikeout, dejando a otros dos en base. Los Yankees acabaron con 7 de 30 con corredores en posición de anotar.
El juez se marcha y el ataque se queda con pocos jugadores
Judge se retiró en la sexta entrada por una contractura en la parte inferior de la pierna derecha que empezó a notar en la primera entrada. Falló dos veces y no volvió al campo, solo siete partidos después de una ausencia de 99 días. Por eso Ramos estaba bateando en su lugar.
El entrenador Aaron Boone describió la noche como una oportunidad perdida, no como un partido robado, y sus palabras reflejaban la importancia del momento en el calendario.
«Obviamente, muchas cosas buenas, pero no las suficientes», dijo Boone. «Ha sido un golpe duro, claro, cuando tenías la oportunidad de barrer la serie y justo antes de un día de descanso. Pero tenemos que superarlo y prepararnos para enfrentarnos a un buen equipo de los Diamondbacks».
Al final del partido, Boone no se anduvo con rodeos con Lombard, pero tampoco lo machacó.
Boone reconoció que la bola de Caratini rebotó en el montículo, pero fue una jugada que Lombard «se espera que haga y sabemos que es capaz de hacer».
Rodón lo da todo en octubre, pero no saca nada a cambio
Carlos Rodón le dio a los Yankees el comienzo que necesita una rotación en la postemporada y vio cómo se esfumaba. El zurdo encajó dos carreras en seis entradas, ampliando su récord de la franquicia a 25 salidas consecutivas en las que ha encajado tres carreras o menos. Lanzó 102 lanzamientos, su máximo de la temporada, y bajó su promedio de carreras limpias a 2,95.
«Empecé un poco lento, un poco tenso», dijo Rodon. «Me fui soltando en las siguientes entradas, así que eso estuvo bien».
Clarke Schmidt hizo su tan esperado regreso en la séptima entrada, ponchando a dos antes de que Brent Headrick dejara a dos en base. El bullpen corrió una maratón que la alineación nunca supo recompensar.
Una primicia para el club que no se veía desde 1991
Este es el dato que pocos destacarán. Ha sido la primera derrota de los Yankees tras ir ganando varias veces en entradas extras desde el 5 de mayo de 1991, en Seattle, es decir, en un lapso de más de 34 años. También fue su octava derrota en la última entrada de la temporada, un récord de la franquicia, y ningún equipo de la MLB ha encajado más hits decisivos en la última entrada en 2026, según datos de Baseball Reference. Ningún equipo de los Yankees ha perdido nunca más partidos a domicilio en entradas extras en una sola temporada.
Lo curioso es que los equipos malos no acumulan cifras como estas. Un equipo mediocre pierde en nueve partidos. Solo un buen equipo es capaz de forzar una prórroga fuera de casa una y otra vez, y luego seguir perdiéndola.
Cómo queda la carrera por la División Este de la Liga Americana
Spencer Jones lanzó su propia advertencia, ponchándose cinco veces en una noche en la que se fue de 0 de 6, lo que demostró lo rápido que se castigan los swings fallidos cuando los márgenes se estrechan. En septiembre se lee de otra manera que en julio.
Los Yankees tienen el jueves libre antes de empezar una serie de fin de semana en Arizona, donde Gerrit Cole será el lanzador titular el viernes a las 21:40 h (hora del Este). No se espera que Judge tenga que hacerse más pruebas. Nueva York ha perdido terreno que quizá no recupere y le ha dado un respiro a los Rays.
Los Yankees saben cómo ganar los partidos intermedios. Una noche en la que solo tenían que ganar uno, no pudieron.
¿Qué te parece? Deja tu comentario aquí abajo.

item.title: [nytimes.com] Yankees mailbag: Aaron Judge’s injury, Jasson Domínguez’s future and the playoff rotation
item.dc:creator: Chris Kirschner

item.content:encoded:
The New York Yankees are now in wait-and-see mode.
Aaron Judge left Wednesday’s game early with right leg tightness. There’s no word yet on whether he’ll have to miss time, and we likely won’t have an answer until Friday at the earliest.
Before then, let’s answer some of your Yankees questions in part one of our mailbag. If you want to ask anything else, there’s still time to do so here.
Note: Questions have been edited for clarity and brevity.
Advertisement
Assuming Trent Grisham is healthy, who starts in center field during the playoffs: him or Spencer Jones? — Ed H.
Yankees manager Aaron Boone told reporters Wednesday that Grisham is running “up to a decent speed” in his comeback from a right hamstring strain. Considering Grisham at normal speed is slow, it’s anyone’s guess what that actually means.
If Grisham is ready to go, it will be interesting to see what Boone decides. There are numerous examples of the Yankees opting for the veteran over an inexperienced player like Jones when the games matter most.
Both players have their warts. Neither Grisham nor Jones is a good defensive center fielder. Jones looked abysmal in center, letting a ground ball go under his glove, dropping a fly ball that hit his glove and nearly trucking Heliot Ramos in right field. Meanwhile, Grisham has trouble getting to balls over his head and in the gaps because he’s slow-footed. There’s likely a higher floor of success, though, for Grisham. Even on the balls Jones has caught, there have been instances where he doesn’t look comfortable reading the play off the bat.
So the main difference will come down to offense.
Before Grisham injured his hamstring, he was not hitting. Calls for Jones to take over were already happening. To Jones’ credit, he has produced at the plate. Even after a dreadful 0-for-6 performance with five strikeouts on Wednesday, Jones has a 113 wRC+. He is always a threat to pop a home run, and that wins ballgames in October.
Grisham has one of the best eyes on the team, rarely strikes out and works at-bats. That matters when the batters behind him would likely be Ben Rice and Judge (depending on his health).
Not that my opinion holds any weight, but I’d stick with Jones in center field. The Yankees can always use Grisham, who’s one of the most clutch hitters on the team, in big spots off the bench.
Advertisement
What will/should the Yankees playoff rotation and bullpen look like? I hate to say it, but Gerrit Cole and Max Fried are not looking like aces these days. The team is winning Will Warren’s and Carlos Rodón’s starts. How are these facts likely to influence Boone’s postseason rotation decisions? … As soon as I say this, Fried pitches a gem. Jinx. — Aaron D.
The American League East race isn’t over yet, but the likeliest outcome is the Yankees will play in a wild-card series against the Boston Red Sox. That means the Yankees will only need three starting pitchers for the first round.
Cam Schlittler should start Game 1. There’s no argument otherwise. Schlittler is one of the very best starting pitchers in the sport. You want your best pitcher going in Game 1 to give yourself the best possible chance of not facing a must-win Game 2.
From there, it’ll be a toss-up between Fried and Cole. Both pitchers have concerns attached to them.
Fried has battled command issues all season, while Cole has allowed plenty of hard contact while not getting much swing-and-miss. I’d lean toward Fried over Cole.
As for the bullpen, the Yankees could have Rodón in case the club needs length. The others likely to be on the roster are Will Warren, David Bednar, Brent Headrick, Paul Blackburn, John Schreiber, Clarke Schmidt, Ryan Yarbrough and Ryan Weathers, if he’s healthy. I’d leave off Tim Hill, who has struggled mightily this season, Luis Gil and Michael Fulmer.
What is the realistic outlook for second base next year? Jazz Chisholm Jr. hasn’t played up to his talent, which might make him more enticing by bringing down his cost. The infield is already crowded, though, with Ryan McMahon under contract, George Lombard Jr.’s promotion, José Caballero, two first basemen (three if Paul Goldschmidt is still seen as Giancarlo Stanton insurance), and Anthony Volpe’s re-ascension. — Marco F.
What the Yankees decide to do at second base is one of the most fascinating storylines of the offseason.
Advertisement
I agree with you, Marco, that this season has likely cost Chisholm millions. He is nearing the end of his worst offensive season since 2021. He won’t reach the heights he set for himself entering 2026, but he still could reach a 20-40 season. Few players have the talent to post those numbers. Before this year, Chisholm posted back-to-back 4+ fWAR seasons. It would not be wrong for the Yankees or another team to bet on his upside.
Chisholm still offers tremendous defense at second and excellent baserunning. If his bat gets back to being considerably above average, he profiles as one of the best second basemen in the sport. There are valid concerns about his offense, though. His hit tool is considerably below average, and as he ages and loses athleticism, that could be a major problem that he cannot overcome.
The Yankees should consider giving Chisholm a short-term deal, though. He is a better option than Caballero and Volpe, who are better as role players, and few available players are better than what he can provide.
The Yankees should strongly consider playing Caballero or Volpe, who played a few games in the minors there, at third base. McMahon is one of the worst everyday regulars in the big leagues this season, and there’s a higher likelihood of Caballero or Volpe producing at the plate.
Has the Martian played his last game in a Yankees uniform? — oconnell13
It’s a hard question to answer because you can’t predict injuries. You never know if the Yankees will have to reach into the minor leagues for depth.
But it’s not far-fetched to think Jasson Domínguez will never play in another important game for the Yankees again. He cannot be trusted in the field. Every game matters for the Yankees, and there’s always a queasy feeling when the ball is hit his way.
His bat also hasn’t progressed enough to keep giving him chances to prove himself. Jones has leapfrogged him on the depth chart, and the Yankees now have Heliot Ramos on their roster. There may not be space for Domínguez.
Advertisement
What are the Yankees’ pitching plans for the rest of the regular season? Specifically, who’s lining up for the Rays series and will any of them be limited in terms of pitch count? — Nick B.
As of now, the Yankees are lined up to start their best four starters against the Rays next week. Here’s how it looks:
Tuesday: Fried and Rodón are in line to start the games of the doubleheader.
Wednesday: Cole
Thursday: Schlittler
The Rays are also on track to start their best pitchers for that series. They could start Nick Martinez and Drew Rasmussen on Tuesday, Freddy Peralta on Wednesday and Ian Seymour on Thursday. Their rotation is dependent on what they decide to do for their weekend series against the Boston Red Sox. But if they wanted, all of these pitchers could factor into their pitching plans next week.
Any chance the Yanks consider Ben Rice as the backup catcher on the postseason roster to free up an extra bench spot for someone more versatile (and better than) Ali Sánchez/J.C. Escarra? — Matthew L.
The odds of this happening are close to zero.
Earlier in the season, Rice kept catching behind the scenes. Before games, he’d catch bullpens and do on-field drills with director of catching Tanner Swanson. Rice hasn’t done any of that in months.
If anything, Rice would only be used in an emergency situation. Believe it or not, the organization believes in Sánchez. That’s why they didn’t promote Mitch Garver. Sánchez is out of minor league options, so they’d have to designate him for assignment and risk him getting claimed off waivers. They value the consistency he provides to their pitchers, and they think he’s a better defender than the metrics show.

item.title: [Claro Sports] Aaron Judge preocupa a los Yankees: sale del partido por una molestia en la pantorrilla derecha
item.dc:creator: Gael Gonzalez Flores
item.description: Los Bombarderos del Bronx esperan la recuperación de su capitán para disputar los playoffs de la MLB La preocupación volvió a aparecer alrededor de Aaron Judge, quien tuvo que abandonar el encuentro entre los New York Yankees y Minnesota Twins debido a una molestia en la parte inferior de la pierna derecha. El jardinero derecho salió del partido durante la sexta entrada de la derrota de Nueva York por 5-4 en extra innings. El capitán de los Yankees fue reemplazado por Heliot Ramos como bateador
item.content:encoded:
Los Bombarderos del Bronx esperan la recuperación de su capitán para disputar los playoffs de la MLB
La preocupación volvió a aparecer alrededor de Aaron Judge, quien tuvo que abandonar el encuentro entre los New York Yankees y Minnesota Twins debido a una molestia en la parte inferior de la pierna derecha. El jardinero derecho salió del partido durante la sexta entrada de la derrota de Nueva York por 5-4 en extra innings.
El capitán de los Yankees fue reemplazado por Heliot Ramos como bateador emergente, después de que en sus dos turnos al bate ante el lanzador Zebby Matthews se fue ponchado. Judge había descansado el martes como parte de la programación del equipo, pero esta vez tuvo que dejar el terreno por precaución.
La molestia apareció durante el desarrollo del partido, aunque Judge no mostró señales evidentes de dolor durante sus acciones defensivas. En la quinta entrada, el pelotero corrió hacia la zona entre los jardines para perseguir un doblete, en la que fue su última participación antes de salir del encuentro.
MÁS INFORMACIÓN: Brewers conquistan por cuarto año consecutivo la División Central de la Liga Nacional
Aaron Judge explica la decisión de abandonar el juego
Después del partido, Aaron Judge explicó que sintió rigidez en la zona afectada desde la primera entrada, pero intentó continuar debido a la importancia de los últimos juegos de la temporada regular.
“Intenté restarle importancia y ver cuánto podía aguantar, ya que estos juegos son importantes en la recta final de la temporada”, señaló Judge. Sin embargo, después de hablarlo con el cuerpo técnico, consideró que lo mejor era abandonar el partido para evitar una situación que pudiera afectar al equipo.
El tres veces ganador del Jugador Más Valioso de la Liga Americana explicó que la decisión tuvo como objetivo no arriesgar una lesión mayor y permitir que otro jugador pudiera ocupar su lugar. “Pensé que lo correcto era salir del juego para no perjudicar al equipo, ya fuera en el campo o en las bases”, comentó el bateador de los Yankees.
Judge también señaló que este tipo de molestias pueden aparecer durante el proceso de recuperación y aumento de intensidad después de una ausencia prolongada. “Van a surgir pequeños inconvenientes como éste. Simplemente pensé que era mejor no forzar la situación”, agregó.
Aaron Boone confirma contractura en la pantorrilla derecha
El manager de los Yankees, Aaron Boone, confirmó que la molestia de Judge corresponde a una contractura en la parte inferior de la pierna derecha, específicamente en la pantorrilla.
El estratega explicó que el pelotero comenzó a sentir la rigidez después de uno de sus turnos al bate y que, tras consultar con el cuerpo médico, se tomó la decisión de retirarlo del partido como medida preventiva.
“Ya ha recibido bastante terapia en la zona tras salir del juego. Mañana jueves continuará bajo estricto tratamiento médico y ahí evaluaremos qué es lo que realmente tenemos”, explicó Boone.
Una de las principales preocupaciones dentro de la organización era conocer si la molestia estaba relacionada con la lesión que mantuvo fuera de actividad a Judge durante varios meses. Sin embargo, Boone aclaró que esta situación no tiene relación con la fractura por estrés en la costilla que sufrió anteriormente.
Yankees esperan contar con Judge para la postemporada
La salida de Judge llega en un momento importante para los Yankees, que ya aseguraron su lugar en la postemporada y se encuentran en la pelea por mejorar su posición dentro de la Liga Americana.
Desde su regreso tras la ausencia por la fractura de costilla, Judge batea de 26-4 con 13 ponches y un extrabase en siete partidos. Además, conectó un cuadrangular durante el primer juego de la serie ante Minnesota, el mismo día en que Nueva York confirmó su clasificación a los playoffs.
Aaron Boone destacó la importancia del jardinero dentro del equipo y aseguró que esperan que pueda recuperarse para ser una pieza importante en octubre. “Obviamente, él es una pieza clave en lo que hacemos. Esperamos tratar la molestia, superarla y que él pueda ser un factor importante en algún momento”, indicó el manager.
Los Yankees tendrán descanso este jueves antes de iniciar una serie como visitantes ante los Arizona Diamondbacks, una ventana que el equipo aprovechará para evaluar la evolución de Judge y determinar los siguientes pasos en su recuperación.

item.title: [The Japan Times] Yankees slugger Aaron Judge exits game against Twins
item.dc:creator: Int-No Author
item.description: New York slugger Aaron Judge exited in the sixth inning of Wednesday’s game against the Minnesota Twins because of tightness in his lower right leg. item.content:encoded:
New York slugger Aaron Judge exited in the sixth inning of Wednesday’s game against the Minnesota Twins because of tightness in his lower right leg.
Judge said he was injured during the first inning and later reported the ailment to manager Aaron Boone, who removed him from the game.
“I tried to play it off and see how long we can go because these games are important down the stretch,” Judge said after a 5-4, 13-inning loss to the Twins. “But talking it over, I thought it would be the right move to come out so we don’t cost the team on the field or cost the team on the basepaths.”
Judge, 34, was playing in his seventh game since returning from a 99-day absence due to a stress fracture in his first right rib.
Boone said he was informed that Judge’s leg “just felt tight” after heading out to right field after batting in the first inning.
“He said he felt a little something after the first inning,” Boone said. “Hopefully it’s something we are able to catch.”
Judge was replaced by pinch hitter Heliot Ramos in the sixth with the Yankees trailing 2-0. Ramos also filled his position in right field.
The Yankees have an off day on Thursday before beginning a three-game series against the host Arizona Diamondbacks. But Judge didn’t think his injury would require any imaging. He said the situation is part of returning from a lengthy time away from the field.
“Once you start ramping up, things pop up,” Judge said. “Hopefully, it’s just one little thing and we’re back out there soon.”
Judge struck out in his two at-bats to lower his average this season to .241 in 66 games. The eight-time All-Star and three-time American League MVP (2022, 2024, 2025) has 18 home runs and 41 RBIs this season.
After missing 84 games since May 31, Judge was 3-for-17 (.176) with no extra-base hits in his first five games back from injury before hitting a three-run homer on Monday as New York clinched a postseason berth with an 8-3 victory over Minnesota.

item.content:encoded:
On Wednesday afternoon, the New York Yankees and Minnesota Twins are finishing their series at Target Field.
The Yankees have won each of the first two games, so they are looking to go for the sweep.
Anthony Volpe finished Saturday’s 8-1 victory with two hits, one walk and one stolen base.
UPDATE: The Yankees lost 5-4 on Wednesday.
Boone Makes Volpe Statement
In a recent interview with Jomboy Media’s Talkin’ Yanks, manager Aaron Boone was asked about Volpe (h/t Talkin’ Yanks).
The 25-year-old hit a grand slam in his first game back at the MLB level (on September 10).
Jomboy: “That was a cool day. It was cool to hear the fans back him, cool to hear his quotes. For me personally, just cool to see a new approach at the plate. Kind of drastically different in terms of a baseball swing. He’s stepping back. You in your quote, said he’s definitely grounding himself more on that back leg. His hands are in a new position. So I was wondering if you could peel back the curtain on how does that new approach happen? Is that minor league coaches? Is that Rowson sending down to the minor league coaches, or is that Volpe on his own?”
Boone: “I think it’s the hitting department, Jarret DeHart getting involved. I don’t think it’s anything drastically new. He’s been that at different times, it’s just getting consistent and getting into a good place down there. And to me, when he came back up, it just looked more grounded. I feel like he’s getting to stronger positions… There’s only been… four, five, six games, so he’s gotten some results, but I also feel like there’s been some swings where he’s just missed… A couple balls deep to right that I feel like he’s kind of on time for and getting into a strong position. I thought last night, coming off the bench, he put a good at-bat where he hits the ball well to left. So those are all good signs that he’s on some things, and he’s doing a good job with the whole field but not sacrificing authority in his swing. He’s getting a good swing off.”
Looking At Volpe
Volpe is in the middle of his fourth season at the MLB level (all with New York).
He came into Wednesday batting .249 with 47 hits, two home runs, 24 RBIs, 23 runs and 10 stolen bases in 62 games.

item.title: [The New York Times] Aaron Judge exits Yankees game with leg injury: ‘We’re still trying to ramp up’
item.dc:creator: Brendan Kuty
item.description: MINNEAPOLIS — There was still a mystery surrounding the injury that forced New York Yankees star Aaron Judge to want to leave the game in the sixth inning of a 5-4, 13-inning loss to the Minnesota Twins on Wednesday. item.content:encoded:
MINNEAPOLIS — There was still a mystery surrounding the injury that forced New York Yankees star Aaron Judge to want to leave the game in the sixth inning of a 5-4, 13-inning loss to the Minnesota Twins on Wednesday.
The Yankees said Judge was dealing with right lower leg tightness, but Judge refused to confirm which leg was troubling him, let alone which part. Instead, Judge said he was dealing with something in his “lower body.”
When asked whether he would go for tests, he said “probably not,” but also, “I have no idea.”
Was Judge concerned? He didn’t say.
Advertisement
“We’re still trying to ramp up,” he said. “So there’s going to be little things like this as they come up. Just thought it would be best (to leave the game) instead of pushing through like I normally do, and it might become a little worse. Get somebody who’s ready to go in there. Trying to do what’s best for the team.”
Judge appeared to limp a little in right field at points during the game. Manager Aaron Boone said the 34-year-old felt discomfort after the first inning, but that he wasn’t told Judge was dealing with anything until just before he took him out of the game.
“He said he felt a little something after the first inning and whenever it was I took him out,” Boone said. “That’s when I was made aware of it and just didn’t want to push through anything, and hopefully it’s something we’re able to catch.”
Judge likened it to an injury “you deal with this every spring training.”
“At the start of the season, once you start ramping up again, things pop up,” he said. “That’s where we’ve been, thankfully, this whole time coming back. Nothing’s really nagged us. Hope this is just one little thing and we’re back out there soon.”
Judge left Wednesday’s game before his at-bat in the sixth inning with a runner on first base, one out and the Yankees trailing 2-0. Heliot Ramos took over for Judge. Judge was 0-for-2 with two swinging strikeouts before exiting. He had Tuesday off.
The Yankees are off Thursday. They play three games on turf at Chase Field against the Arizona Diamondbacks starting Friday.
His early exit is likely worrisome to Yankees fans, who waited more than three months for his return from a stress fracture in his first right rib. He rejoined the lineup Sept. 8. That day, Boone removed him after six innings, and Judge said he was “not happy” about the decision, wanting to play a full nine innings despite having not played since May 31.
Advertisement
Judge declined to take a rehab assignment before returning from his rib injury. Instead, he took a round of live batting practice, hit off a high-velocity pitching machine and had a coach hit fly balls to him.
Since returning, he is just 4-for-23 (.173), with his sole home run coming Monday, helping the Yankees clinch an American League playoff spot.
The Yankees have 10 regular-season games remaining, and they are four games behind the AL East division-leading Tampa Bay Rays, whom they host for a four-game set next week.
“I kind of tried to play it off and see how we go because these games are important down the stretch,” he said. “Kind of talked it over, thought it would be the right move to come out so we don’t cost the team in the field or cost the team on the base paths.”

item.title: [bolavip.com] Aaron Judge injury update: NY Yankees’ Aaron Boone reveals next steps after early exit vs Twins

item.content:encoded:
Aaron Judge was pulled early and his injury update was revealed as the New York Yankees fell in extra innings to the Minnesota Twins by a score of 5-4. While falling just short of the sweep stings, it all feels minuscule as the Bronx Bombers feared losing their best player right before the 2026 MLB postseason. Based on Aaron Boone’s initial reaction, that bullet may have been dodged. Judge eased the Yankees’ concerns with an encouraging injury update, too.
Still, it should serve as a wake-up call for New York. Moving forward, Yankees manager Boone laid out a clear work plan for Judge, who’s suffered a setback less than 10 days after his return from the 60-day injured list (IL). The fact that his latest issue has nothing to do with the previous lengthy stress fracture in his rib is, at the very least, alarming.
“Lower leg, yeah. [Judge] will get treatment and stuff. Obviously, already has had a lot of treatment. Treatment tomorrow and we’ll see what we got,” Boone said about Judge’s injury in the mid-innings against the Twins on Wednesday afternoon.
Judge speaks on injury
Although it was Judge himself who told Boone and the Yankees’ medical team about the tightness in his lower body midway through the series finale against the Twins, the three-time MVP admitted it wasn’t until after a while of testing things out that he decided enough was enough.
Manager Aaron Boone #17 of the New York Yankees walks.
“[I first felt something in my lower leg] there in the first inning,” Judge said, via YES Network. “I tried to kind of play it off and see how long it’d go because this game was very important down the stretch. Talked it over, thought it’d be the right move to come out so we don’t cost the team. I didn’t want to cost the team down the road. I can’t pinpoint it [to a certain play or movement.]”
Luckily for New York and Judge, he didn’t aggravate anything, but the fact that he was still out there in the field and at the plate while dealing with an announced discomfort is less than ideal. Things could have ended much worse for the Yankees, and they still have yet to run tests and hear the results on Judge’s right-leg injury. That is if Judge even goes through evaluations.
Will Judge be sidelined?
According to Boone’s postgame comments, that remains pretty much up in the air. For the time being, New York is confident it has avoided a serious injury, but a brief hiatus in Judge’s return may still be in order.
“I don’t know [if Judge will miss games]. We’ll see. We have an off day tomorrow, so I’m not going to speculate one way or the other,” Boone commented.
The Yankees’ next game is on Sept. 18 when they start a brand-new, three-game series against the Arizona Diamondbacks on the road. It will be the Pinstripers’ last road trip of the 2026 MLB regular season before a seven-game homestand at Yankee Stadium to close out the campaign.

item.content:encoded:
Yankees news: Aaron Boone drops big Trent Grisham injury update appeared first on ClutchPoints. Add ClutchPoints as a Preferred Source by clicking here.
New York Yankees manager Aaron Boone provided a positive update on Trent Grisham's injury recovery on Wednesday.
The 29-year-old was placed on the injured list on September 5 after being diagnosed with a Grade 2 right hamstring strain. When the injury was initially diagnosed, Boone acknowledged that Grisham could potentially miss the rest of the regular season.
Speaking ahead of their game against the Minnesota Twins, Boone said the outfielder has reached "a pretty decent speed" in his running progression while also participating in baseball activities, per Gary Phillips. His return date remains uncertain, but his recent rehabilitation progress has given him a chance to return.
Watch sports LIVE with fuboTV (free trial)
Grisham's absence has opened the door for Spencer Jones to take over as the Yankees' everyday center fielder. During that stretch, Jones has batted .382 with two home runs, 10 RBIs and seven runs scored in his last 10 games. He is also slashing .361/.425/.528 across 10 games since assuming Grisham's spot.
Jones has maintained his defensive role while producing offensively, although he has recorded a 34.9% strikeout rate. He also hit a three-run homer during Tuesday night's win over the Twins.
The situation could create a major playing-time decision if Grisham returns. After hitting a career-best 34 home runs in 2025, Grisham is batting only .211 with a 95 OPS+ this season. His -8 defensive runs saved rank second-worst among qualified center fielders.
Still, Boone has continued to express confidence in Grisham and considers him a valuable player overall. Meanwhile, Jones' recent surge could give the Yankees another option in center field when Grisham becomes available.
Related: Yankees rookie Spencer Jones joins Aaron Judge club nobody wants in loss to Twins
Related: Yankees' Aaron Judge shares his side of story about leg tightness concern

item.content:encoded:
MINNEAPOLIS -- The first two games of this week’s series at Target Field couldn’t have gone much better for the Yankees. They won both handily, and on Monday Aaron Judge hit his first home run since returning from the IL on Sept. 8.
Judge, who sat out Tuesday’s game as a routine day off after playing six straight games, struck out in each of his first two at-bats against Twins starter Zebby Matthews on Wednesday. After the game, he said he felt a stiffness in his lower right leg in the first inning.
“I tried to kind of play it off and see how long we could go, because these games are important down the stretch,” Judge said. “But kind of talking it over, I thought it'd be the right move to come out, so I don't cost the team on the field or cost the team on the basepath.”
With an off-day scheduled for Thursday, the team will wait to issue any prognosis on the severity of the injury until after he’s received extensive treatment over the next 48 hours.
“We’re not going to speculate one way or the other. We’ll just see how he responds,” manager Aaron Boone said.
Judge, who said he didn’t anticipate getting testing done, said he couldn’t pinpoint any specific activity or movement that triggered the stiffness, but the feeling isn’t an unfamiliar one to him.
“I feel like you deal with this every Spring Training. You know, usually at the start of the season once you start ramping up again, things pop up, and that's where we've been,” Judge said. “Thankfully, this whole time coming back, nothing's really nagged us. So hopefully it's just one little thing and then we're back out there soon.”
It would be a huge blow to the team to lose Judge after just getting him back into the lineup for the first time in three months. But at the same time, professional athletes and their coaches have to keep an eye on the big picture, and one Wednesday afternoon game against the Twins in mid-September pales in importance compared to upcoming series against the Diamondbacks, Rays and Orioles, plus whatever postseason action the team might see.
That’s especially true when that four-game series against Tampa Bay starting Tuesday could still determine the AL East champions -- and potentially a first-round bye in the postseason.
“Obviously he’s a key figure of what we do,” Boone said. “Hopefully we get it treated and knock it out and be a factor at some point.”
Heliot Ramos pinch-hit for Judge and also struck out against Matthews, who fanned eight in six scoreless innings. Ramos would likely fill in for Judge in right field during any absence he might incur.
The Yankees certainly could have used Judge’s bat in the lineup as they traded blows with the Twins in extra innings, after Anthony Volpe smacked a game-tying double off the wall in the top of the ninth with his club down to its final out.
In the 12th, the Yanks squandered an opportunity with the bases loaded and nobody out, as Ramos grounded into a double play, with Volpe thrown out at home plate. Ali Sánchez then struck out to end the threat, before Twins pinch-hitter Victor Caratini delivered a walk-off single up the middle in the 13th.

item.content:encoded:
New York Yankees star Aaron Judge exited Wednesday’s 5-4 loss to the Minnesota Twins at Target Field in the sixth inning with right lower leg tightness, according to multiple reports.
Following Wednesday’s game, Yankees manager Aaron Boone was asked about Judge’s injury.
New York Yankees’ Aaron Boone Makes Aaron Judge Statement Amid Injury News
“I was made aware of [the injury] right before he came out. He said he felt a little something after the first inning, and whenever it was I took him out, that’s when I was made aware of it, and I just didn’t want to push through anything. Hopefully it’s something we’re able to catch.”
Boone said he doesn’t know if Judge will have to miss games.
Looking at Aaron Judge
Judge started Wednesday’s game as the right fielder. The outfielder hit third in the lineup before being replaced by Heliot Ramos in the sixth inning.
Judge went 0-for-2 with two strikeouts in Wednesday’s game.
Aaron Judge missed most the season with a right rib stress fracture. New York placed him on the IL on June 2. He didn’t return until Sept. 7.
Judge has struggled since returning from the IL, hitting just .190/.227/.333 with one home run and three RBI over six games.
Before being placed on the IL, Judge hit .248/.375/.533 with 17 home runs and 38 RBI over 59 games this season.
Since making his MLB debut in 2016, Judge has slashed .291/.410/.610 with 386 home runs and 871 RBI. He has won three AL MVP Awards.
New York Yankees Right Now
The Yankees won the first two games of their series against the Twins before losing the finale 5-4 in extra innings on Wednesday.
The Yankees’ record dropped to 88-64 after the loss. New York is now four-games behind the Tampa Bay Rays for first place in the American League East. The club has a 5 1/2-game lead over the Boston Red Sox for the first AL Wild Card spot.
Next, the Yankees will begin a three-game series against the Arizona Diamondbacks in Phoenix on Friday after an off day on Thursday.

item.content:encoded:
With the postseason less than two weeks away, the Yankees are left holding their breath regarding the status of their slugging captain, Aaron Judge, who left Wednesday’s game against the Minnesota Twins early with what the team described as right lower-leg tightness.
Judge, who started the game in right field, was seen wincing during his second and final at-bat of the afternoon in the top of the third inning following a check-swing. He was pinch-hit for by Heliot Ramos in the top of the sixth, sending up immediate red flags for a team fighting to catch the Tampa Bay Rays for the top spot in the American League East.
Manager Aaron Boone said that Juge felt something in the first inning and took him out to make sure he didn’t “push through anything.”
He will undergo treatment, and the team will get a better sense of how severe the issue is on Thursday.
There may be some relief in that it is not his rib or oblique that is bothering him, though such a statement is a bit premature, considering the specifics of this lower-leg issue is unknown. Judge has already missed three months this season due to a rib injury that kept him out from late May to Sept. 7.
Wednesday’s game was just his seventh game back from the injured list, and he has struggled mightily after the long layoff, going 4-for-23 (.173) with one home run, three RBI, and 13 strikeouts.
Boone previously stated that he was going to take things slow with Judge because they forewent a rehab assignment. But he played six straight games before getting Tuesday off — the day after New York clinched its ninth postseason berth in 10 years.
The prospect of being without Judge this postseason should be a daunting one for the Yankees. Their offense struggled mightily without him, scoring 341 runs in the 84 games without him (4.06 runs per game). Only the Cincinnati Reds, Toronto Blue Jays, Cleveland Guardians, Los Angeles Angels, and Seattle Mariners scored fewer runs in all of baseball during that stretch.
Still, the Bronx Bombers should like their chances regardless of the status of their captain. The American League is exceptionally poor this season, with only six teams possessing records over .500. Three of them, including the Yankees, inhabit the AL East.
They also have one of the most imposing pitching staffs in all of baseball, as they are set to trot out AL Cy Young favorite Cam Schlittler, Gerrit Cole, Max Fried, and Carlos Rodon in a shortened postseason rotation.

item.content:encoded:
MINNESOTA — Aaron Judge’s health has the Yankees holding their breath once again.
The slugger left Wednesday’s 5-4, 13-inning loss to the Twins prematurely when Heliot Ramos pinch-hit for him with a runner on and one out in the top of the sixth inning. The Yankees were only down two runs at the time, and Judge, initially expected to rest on Wednesday, was fresh off an off day.
A short time later, the Yankees announced that Judge exited the game with tightness in his right lower leg. The news comes with the right fielder just seven games removed from a 99-day absence for a stress fracture in his first right rib.
“Hopefully, it’s something we were able to catch,” Aaron Boone said after the game.
Neither Boone nor Judge specified what part of the body the latter hurt. Judge, always unrevealing when it comes to his injuries, wouldn’t even say it was his leg, stating he simply had a “lower body” issue.
Judge did say that he first felt something while playing the field in the first inning on Wednesday, but he couldn’t pinpoint a particular play. Boone said he no knowledge of an injury prior to Wednesday, and that he wasn’t made aware of the problem until he noticed Judge hobbling in the outfield on a play he wasn’t involved in during the bottom of the fifth inning.
Judge also appeared to grimace when he took a check swing on the first pitch of his third-inning at-bat.
“I tried to kind of play it off and see how long we could go, because these games are important down the stretch,” Judge said. “But in talking it over, I thought it’d be the right move to come out so we don’t cost the team in the field or on the basepaths.
“I didn’t think it was smart to push it too much here.”
There is no update on Aaron Judge as of this moment
🎥: @YESNetwork pic.twitter.com/hifw6hg9W5
— FOX Sports: MLB (@MLBONFOX) September 16, 2026
Judge is facing his latest injury scare with just 10 games left in the regular season. The Yankees have the day off on Thursday before beginning a three-game series at Arizona’s Chase Field, a turfed surface that wouldn’t be friendly to a lower body injury. The second-place Yanks, who have already secured a playoff berth, will then host a crucial four-game series against the division-leading Rays from Sept. 22-24.
With the off day on Thursday, the Yankees will see how Judge responds to treatment. He said “I don’t know” and “probably not” when asked if he’ll get testing, though Boone wasn’t sure about that.
“Hopefully it’s just one little thing,” Judge said, “and then we’re back out there soon.”
Judge likened his leg issue to the types of nagging injuries that pop up during spring training and at the start of the season when players are ramping up their bodies. He has been doing just that since returning from his rib injury on Sept. 8.
“We’re still trying to ramp up, so there’s going to be little things like this that come up,” Judge said. “I just thought it’d be best to — instead of pushing through it like I normally do, and it might become a little worse — get somebody who’s ready to go in there and just try and do what’s best for the team.”
It should be noted that Judge’s rib rehab and pre-activation build-up skipped some steps. He got his wish after repeatedly making it clear that he wanted to forego a minor league rehab assignment despite missing over three months. The superstar also only faced living pitching once, and that came against some minor leaguers.
Asked if Wednesday’s injury made him rethink the process, Judge told the Daily News, “People blow out their calves and blow out their quads in rehab assignments, so I don’t think taking a game in Double-A will change any of that.”
He added that he felt his build-up has been gradual, as he had felt asymptomatic for weeks before returning.
“That’s what we kind of did with playing the [seven] innings, playing the eight innings,” Judge said, referring to his planned early exits in his first two games back, the first of which he said he was “not happy” about the night of.
Judge also had off on Sept. 10.
Prior to Wednesday, Boone had said that he’s been “pleased” with the way Judge has been responding physically since returning to game action. Judge, who has said he wants to be playing every day, said much of the same over the weekend.
The captain, who went 0-for-2 with two strikeouts before departing on Wednesday, hasn’t had much success at the plate since coming off the injured list as he searches for his timing. He did crush a three-run homer in Monday’s victory over the Twins, but he entered that game 3-for-17 (.176) with zero extra-base hits in his first five games back.
Still, the Yankees have been thrilled to have Judge back in a lineup that struggled mightily without him. With Judge’s mere presence impacting the way those around him are attacked, the Bombers had one of the worst offenses in baseball while the back-to-back MVP was on the IL, ranking last in K% (26.1%); 29th in wRC+ (90) and average (.227); 28th in wOBA (.299); 27th in OPS (.681); and 24th in runs scored (341) from June 2 through Sept. 7.
“I’m not sure exactly what’s going on, but it’s never good when your best player on your team comes out of the lineup,” Carlos Rodón said after battling some velocity issues and tightness of his own on Wednesday. “So obviously, I’m hoping he’s gonna be okay. I’m not sure exactly what’s happening, but I’m sure he’ll be fine.”
While it’s too soon to know if Judge will miss extended time, the Yankees will have limited options for his roster spot if that’s the case. There’s fellow outfielder Jasson Domínguez, but he cannot be trusted to play defense in the critical games that are coming up.
Utilityman Max Schuemann is another choice at Triple-A who can also play the outfield.
Of course, the Yankees are hoping it doesn’t come to that.
“Obviously, he’s a key figure to what we do,” Boone said. “Hopefully, we get it treated and knock it out and [he can] be a factor at some point.”

item.content:encoded:
Yankees RHP Clarke Schmidt Returns As Reliever After 14-Month Rehab
The New York Yankees returned right-handed pitcher Clarke Schmidt from his rehabilitation assignment and reinstated him from the injured list on Wednesday, aiming to integrate the 30-year-old into their bullpen for the postseason following his 14-month recovery from elbow surgery.
Schmidt had an internal brace procedure on his ulnar collateral ligament on July 11, 2025, and began minor league rehab on Aug. 29. The 2017 first-round draft pick was used exclusively as a starter since 2023, but with Cam Schlittler, Max Fried, Carlos Rodon and Gerrit Cole in the rotation, Schmidt will transition to relief.
"It's been a long journey, a lot of work that goes into this. A lot of long days, early mornings," Schmidt said before the game Wednesday against the Minnesota Twins. "I've just been itching to come back."
The Yankees designated popular multi-position player Oswaldo Cabrera for assignment to make room on the 40-man roster for Schmidt. Cabrera missed most of the 2025 season with a severe ankle injury.
"I’m blessed to have a lot of guys on this team that you just admire and respect and love doing the job with on a daily basis," manager Aaron Boone said. "Oswaldo’s right there at the top of that list."
Reporting by The Associated Press.

item.title: [southshorepress.com] Spencer Jones Has Arrived — And the Yankees Better Notice

item.content:encoded:
Spencer Jones Has Arrived — And the Yankees Better Notice
For anyone who might have doubted it, let’s be perfectly clear: Spencer Jones has arrived.
The highly touted Yankees prospect came through the minor leagues with some major question marks. His large stature and concerns about his hit tool led some to wonder whether he would ever consistently make enough contact to become an everyday player.
But the athletic ability and big-time power were always enticing enough for the Yankees to give him his opportunity.
During his first stint in the majors, the strikeout issues were certainly noticeable, and the questions only got louder. Could Jones really handle a full-time role? Were there simply too many holes in his swing?
Well, we can officially put those questions to rest.
Because Jones has taken off.
Jones is batting .346 with five home runs and a .933 OPS over his last 25 games. He is also hitting over .300 with an OPS above .900 over his last 35 games.
And the best part may be yet to come.
Jones is batting a ridiculous .435 with a 1.251 OPS against left-handed pitching this season, both lead MLB (min 50 PA).
That number should get everyone’s attention.
There were questions about whether Jones might eventually become a platoon player or fall into the dreaded “three true outcomes” category — a player whose game revolves around home runs, walks and strikeouts.
Instead, we are seeing something much more complete.
Jones brings excellent defense and the ability to run, along with the power that made him such an intriguing prospect in the first place. When you put all of that together, you are looking at a player who is beginning to look an awful lot like a true five-tool talent.
And that changes things for the Yankees.
When Trent Grisham returns, there will be decisions to make. But after watching what Jones has done lately, there should be no more wondering whether he belongs in the conversation.
Spencer Jones has answered the questions the best way a baseball player can.
He has gone out and hit.
Now, let’s hope the Yankees, and Aaron Boone, realize what they have.

item.title: [theleadsm.com] Cam Schlittler Has a Strong Case for MVP

item.content:encoded:
The American League Cy Young race is over. In his last start, Cam Schlittler twirled a six-inning, one-hit, eight-strikeout gem against the Mets. In fact, ESPN’s award tracker no longer has odds for the race.
With the Yankees also clinching a playoff berth with their win Monday night, there’s not much left at stake in New York’s regular season. Except for Schlittler’s potential run at being the first pitcher to win MVP since 2014.
Schlittler has two starts remaining this year. Barring Aaron Boone toying with the rotation to line them up for the postseason, he’s scheduled to get the ball for game two in Arizona on Sept. 19 and game four against the Rays on Sept. 24.
The Statistical Case
There’s a long list of stats you can cite to put Schlittler’s dominance this season in context. There are a few worth highlighting.
Schlittler’s ERA is currently an AL-best 1.95. That’s the lowest ERA of any qualified Yankees starter since Ron Guidry (1.74)in 1978. The next most recent sub-two ERA in Yankee history is 1943 Spud Chandler (1.64). He also has a marginally better ERA than Jacob Misiorowski, the NL frontrunner for Cy Young.
While they both display a 1.95 ERA, the formula for ERA actually allows for the
Schlittler also has a better ERA+ than .
ERA+ adjusts to the league, wherein league average is always 100. That means Schlittler has been 116% better than league average, while Kershaw was “only” 97% better. Schlittler has also done this in 31 starts, while Kershaw has done it in only 27.
Finally, he currently leads the American League in Wins Above Replacement. Yordan Alvarez (5.8), the odds-on favorite, Junior Caminero (5.3), the home run leader, and Bobby Witt Jr. (6.3) all trail Schlittler’s mark of 7.1. In an award measuring value, Schlittler has statistically impacted his team the most.
The last time a pitcher won MVP was Kershaw in 2014. Spud Chandler also won in 1943, and Guidry finished second in 1978.
The Comparative Case
The American League MVP race at this point is down to five names. Schlittler, Alvarez, Caminero, Witt Jr. and rookie sensation Kevin McGonigle.
Players like Ben Rice and Dillon Dingler were in the thick of the race, but recently played themselves out with .641 and .518 OPS in August, respectively.
Yordan Alvarez
Alvarez is still the favorite, per ESPN. He currently leads baseball in on-base percentage (.427) and slugging percentage (.589), and the American League in batting average (.310). Since his debut in 2019, he has done nothing but mash at the plate, with 2026 his best and healthiest season yet.
It’s hard enough for a primary DH to win MVP. Of course, Ohtani’s done it four of the last five years, but Alvarez isn’t stealing 50 bases or throwing 100 innings. In fact, .
He’s also been abysmal down the stretch. Over the last calendar month (Aug. 15 – Sept. 15) he’s slashed just .238/.375/.393 with two homers and eight RBI. He was once poised to run away with the triple crown, and now it looks like a long shot.
The triple crown is Alvarez’s best bet. If he can turn around these remaining 12 games and reclaim the home run and RBI title, his case is as good as gold. As it stands, Alvarez and Rice are tied for second with 38 home runs to Caminero’s 40. Pete Alonso leads the way with 100 runs driven in, with Alvarez (96) and Caminero (95) close behind.
Junior Caminero
Caminero has been phenomenal in just his 22-year-old season. He’s one of the league’s premier sluggers, hitting 40 homers in 2025 and 2026. He’s a cornerstone on the first-place Tampa Bay Rays.
The main argument against Caminero mirrors Alvarez’s: his game is very one-dimensional. While his hitting prowess is undeniable, he is a negative asset on the base paths and at third base. Unlike Alvarez, he hasn’t cooled off in the final weeks of summer, but at no point this season has he had a narrative driving his MVP case home.
Caminero would surely be a worthy winner. He is a three-true-outcome generator; his batting average sits at a respectable .279.
Bobby Witt Jr.
Then there’s Bobby Witt Jr. He finished second in voting in 2024 and fourth in 2025. He’s perhaps the most well-rounded five -tool player in the league. His game really has no weakness.
2026 could be classified as a “down-year” for him, with “only” a .280 batting average and 18 home runs. He missed about two weeks toward the end of July, so his counting stats aren’t in their usual spot. He doesn’t lead the league in batting, stolen bases, or hits as he has in years past.
He’ll undoubtedly finish towards the top of the ballot, but it’s hard to imagine voters choosing 2026 to reward him. His fifth-place Royals also won’t help his case, especially against the Yankees, Rays and Astros, all currently in a playoff position.
Kevin McGonigle
McGonigle’s rookie season has been excellent. He has split time at shortstop and third base for the Tigers. His offensive profile fits a seasoned veteran. An incredibly balanced slash line of .273/.373/.425 with a nearly even ratio of strikeouts (89) to walks (88). His 6.6 WAR leads position players, but an MLB rookie has only won MVP twice, and not since Ichiro Suzuki in 2001.
It’s hard to imagine a world where McGonigle finds his way atop the voting. Like Witt, he does not lead in any statistical category. His first season in the big leagues has been great, and it’s not far-fetched to say he will take home the award one day, but he will probably finish fifth or sixth in 2026.
Case Closed?
While Aaron Boone endorses his ace as the MVP, teammate and three-time MVP Aaron Judge doesn’t.
“They’ve got a Cy Young Award for a reason, best pitcher in the game. He’s got my vote, definitely, for the Cy Young,” Judge said.
Ultimately, the final two weeks of the season carry a lot of weight. If Yordan Alvarez can turn his bat back on and secure the triple crown, Schlittler stands no chance. If he stays cool and Schlittler has two strong outings left in him, then it might be time to see baseball’s next MVP pitcher.

item.content:encoded:
The New York Yankees have already clinched the postseason, but still have a lot more to play for as they try to go for the sweep on Wednesday afternoon against the Minnesota Twins.
They’re coming off an 8-1 victory over the Twins on Tuesday night in a game in which infielder Anthony Volpe recorded two hits to continue his strong stretch since being recalled on Sept. 10.
However, ahead of Wednesday’s game, Yankees manager Aaron Boone decided to make a notable lineup move involving Volpe.
Yankees Announce Volpe Move
After spending his last few games batting in the seven-hole and clearly adapting just fine at the plate, Boone has decided to move Volpe back down to the nine spot for the series finale.
Other notable lineup changes include superstar Aaron Judge rejoining the lineup after a night off, catcher Austin Wells replacing Ali Sanchez behind the plate, and Jose Caballero getting the day off.
Here’s the full Yankees lineup:
Via Underdog MLB: “Yankees 9/16 B. Rice DH C. Bellinger LF A. Judge RF L. García Jr. 1B S. Jones CF G. Lombard Jr. SS R. McMahon 3B A. Wells C A. Volpe 2B C. Rodón SP.”
Yankees 9/16
B. Rice DH
C. Bellinger LF
A. Judge RF
L. García Jr. 1B
S. Jones CF
G. Lombard Jr. SS
R. McMahon 3B
A. Wells C
A. Volpe 2B
C. Rodón SP
— Underdog MLB (@UnderdogMLB) September 16, 2026
Volpe’s 2026 Season
It’s been a challenging 2026 season for Volpe, who’s in his fourth year with the Yankees.
He began the season on the IL, and for the bulk of his campaign in the majors, he just hasn’t been able to find much of a rhythm.
Entering Wednesday, Volpe has found success since the Yankees sent him to Triple-A on Aug. 4 and recalled him last week, but he still owns a .249 average across 62 games and 189 at-bats. He has recorded 23 runs, 47 hits, two home runs, and 24 RBIs while slugging .344 with a .676 OPS.
Despite this, he has an opportunity down the stretch of the regular season to prove why he belongs on the postseason roster and become an everyday-type player.

item.title: [Pinstripes Nation] Gerrit Cole Ya No Es Una Elección Segura Ahora Que Los Yankees Se Están Replanteando Su Plan De Pitcheo Para La Postemporada
item.dc:creator: Sara Molnick

item.content:encoded:
NUEVA YORK — Durante casi toda la última década, a Gerrit Cole le tocaban automáticamente los partidos más importantes de los Yankees.
Esa seguridad se ha esfumado.
A menos de dos semanas de que termine octubre, el lanzador que marcaba la diferencia en el equipo se ha convertido en su mayor incógnita. La velocidad sigue ahí, pero los resultados se han deteriorado en el peor momento posible. Aaron Boone ha intentado restarle importancia a la preocupación. Pero lo que pasa sigue haciendo que eso sea cada vez más difícil.
Cole, ganador del Premio Cy Young de los Yankees en 2023, ha encajado siete jonrones en sus dos últimas salidas, la cifra más alta en cualquier racha de dos salidas de su carrera, según MLB.com. El que antes era una apuesta segura para el primer partido ha bajado puestos en la jerarquía de octubre y ha generado un auténtico debate sobre si debería ser el lanzador titular en un partido a vida o muerte.
Para un equipo de los Yankees que tiene el mejor promedio de carreras limpias permitidas (ERA) del béisbol, esto es como una grieta en los cimientos. Nueva York se aseguró el lunes su plaza en los playoffs y ahora tiene un balance de 88-63. El pitcheo es la razón por la que el club cree que puede llegar lejos. Se suponía que Cole iba a ser el pilar de esa fortaleza, no que se convirtiera en su mayor incertidumbre.
Un problema mental que aterroriza a los Yankees
El 6 de septiembre, Cole encajó jonrones de los tres primeros bateadores de los Padres a los que se enfrentó. Fernando Tatis Jr., Jake Cronenworth y Manny Machado conectaron tres jonrones seguidos.
Seis días después, los Mets le dieron una paliza al as de los Yankees en una goleada por 12-2. Francisco Lindor conectó un jonrón con el tercer lanzamiento de Cole. Más tarde, el novato Carson Benge también le mandó la pelota fuera del campo con un slider. Cole aguantó 4 1/3 entradas, encajó cinco carreras y tres jonrones, y se llevó abucheos al salir del campo.
Tras el partido, su explicación hizo que la derrota de los Yankees pareciera aún peor.
Cole tiene una efectividad de 6,08 en sus últimas cuatro salidas, con 17 ponches en 22 2/3 entradas, y ha encajado al menos tres carreras limpias en cuatro partidos seguidos.
En lo que va de temporada, tiene un balance de 8-9, con una efectividad de 3,67 y 20 jonrones permitidos en 115 1/3 entradas. Los Yankees solo han promediado 3,67 carreras en sus salidas, lo que ha convertido partidos que antes parecían pan comido en auténticas loterías.
Lo que realmente preocupa a los Yankees
La preocupación no es que Cole haya perdido de repente su nivel de Grandes Ligas. Es por qué los bateadores se ven tan cómodos frente a él.
Los analistas de YES Network, David Cone y Paul O’Neill, plantearon la posibilidad de que Cole esté delatando sus lanzamientos, lo que podría explicar por qué los bateadores han sabido manejar una bola rápida que sigue alcanzando las 98 mph.
El entrenador de lanzadores, Matt Blake, no lo descartó.
«Es posible», dijo Blake, y añadió que «esa es una de las cosas que vamos a analizar».
Blake también señaló un problema más sencillo. Cole está lanzando strikes a un ritmo sin precedentes en su carrera, pero demasiados se quedan en el centro del strike zone.
«Tenemos que sacar la bola de la parte más ancha del plato», dijo Blake. «Además, quizá tengamos que mejorar la ejecución con dos strikes para lanzar a mejores zonas».
Cole ha reconocido el problema sin pretender haberlo resuelto.
«Hay que empezar a hacer ajustes», dijo Cole.
También rechazó la teoría de que delata sus lanzamientos, diciendo que sus lanzamientos deberían seguir dándonos margen incluso si los bateadores los anticipan.
«Aunque sepan (lo que viene), sigue siendo difícil de batear», dijo Cole. «Mis lanzamientos deberían darnos más margen de error».
Cómo está cambiando la rotación
La mala racha de Cole ha trastocado la jerarquía de la rotación.
Cam Schlittler, en una segunda temporada espectacular, se ha revelado como el mejor lanzador del equipo y un probable candidato al premio Cy Young de la Liga Americana. Se perfila como el abridor del primer partido. Max Fried, que vuelve tras una lesión en el codo, y Carlos Rodón tienen ambos un promedio de carreras limpias por debajo de 3,00 y parecen opciones más seguras para los primeros partidos de la serie.
El enfrentamiento complica aún más las cosas. Es probable que los Yankees se enfrenten a Boston en una serie de comodín al mejor de tres. Cole tiene una efectividad de 5,30 en su carrera contra los Red Sox, y solo los Mets le han bateado con más fuerza.
El veterano columnista Joel Sherman resumió la cuestión de octubre en una sola palabra: «correa». Según su hipótesis, Cole empezaría un partido de mitad de temporada con mucho menos margen de error.
«Creo que Schlittler, Fried y Cole van a ser los titulares», dijo Sherman. «La diferencia es que a Cole le van a dar muy, muy poco margen, algo que, por lo general, no habría tenido».
Sherman también vinculó directamente el techo de los Yankees en la postemporada a que Cole y Aaron Judge recuperen su mejor forma.
«Los Yankees podrían quedarse fuera de los playoffs en menos de 48 horas o podrían ganar la Serie Mundial», dijo Sherman. «Ambas opciones están sobre la mesa y las posibilidades de éxito aumentan mucho más si Cole y Judge se ponen las pilas en las próximas dos semanas, porque son Gerrit Cole y Aaron Judge, y son grandes jugadores cuando están en forma».
Los datos sobre los lanzamientos con efecto explican el colapso
Cole ha mantenido a los bateadores zurdos en un OPS de 0,683. El problema son los bateadores diestros, que tienen un slugging de 0,448 contra él, la cifra más alta que han registrado los diestros en cualquier temporada de su carrera.
Las bolas con efecto del as de los Yankees son las que están causando más daño. Los bateadores diestros tienen un promedio de slugging de 0,652 contra su curva, con diferencia la peor cifra de su carrera. Tienen un promedio de slugging de 0,463 contra su slider, también un récord personal y, con holgada diferencia, su peor marca como jugador de los Yankees.
Además, esos lanzamientos están fallando menos. Su curva solo ha generado un 17 % de fallos contra los bateadores diestros, mientras que su slider se sitúa en el 25 %. Además, está lanzando el slider en el centro de la zona contra los bateadores diestros con la mayor frecuencia de su carrera, lo que explica tanto la reducción de los fallos como los contactos más fuertes.
Los modelos de calidad de los lanzamientos muestran el mismo deterioro. El slider de Cole ha bajado de una puntuación de 125 en Stuff+ en 2020 a 106 esta temporada. La curva de la estrella de los Yankees ha bajado de 120 a 104. Ambas siguen estando por encima de la media, pero el margen que antes le hacía imparable se ha reducido.
Cole cumplió 36 años el 8 de septiembre y está en su primera temporada tras recuperarse de una operación de Tommy John, un año que, según la medicina deportiva, suele ser menos brillante que el segundo. Ya sea por un problema mecánico, por delatar sus lanzamientos o por simple cansancio, Nueva York tiene menos de dos semanas para encontrar la respuesta.
Por ahora, el as que en su día se encargaba de las tareas más importantes está haciendo una prueba para un papel en octubre que antes dominaba.
¿Qué te parece? Deja tu comentario más abajo.

item.title: [Pinstripes Nation] Seis Bajas En Los Yankees En 15 Días: ¿qué Hay Detrás De Los Cambios Radicales De Cashman En El Departamento De Ojeadores Internacionales?
item.dc:creator: Inna Zeyger

item.content:encoded:
BRONX, N.Y. — Los Yankees ya se han asegurado una plaza en la postemporada y siguen a 3 1/2 partidos del Tampa Bay en la División Este de la Liga Americana. Pero una de las decisiones más importantes que ha tomado la organización este mes de septiembre no tiene nada que ver con la alineación de Aaron Boone ni con los planes de pitcheo para octubre.
Esto ha dado lugar a seis despidos en lo que va de septiembre.
Todo esto está pasando a miles de millas del Yankee Stadium, en la República Dominicana, Venezuela y otros mercados donde se descubre a los futuros Yankees años antes de que la mayoría de los aficionados sepan siquiera sus nombres.
De esa cantera salieron Robinson Canó, Alfonso Soriano, Gary Sánchez e Iván Nova. Los Yankees siguieron invirtiendo ahí a medida que cambiaban las normas sobre bonificaciones, la tecnología y los métodos de evaluación de jugadores amateurs.
La presión sobre esa área lleva meses aumentando. Donny Rowland, director de ojeadores internacionales desde hacía mucho tiempo, no renovó su contrato cuando este expiró en noviembre. Los Yankees ascendieron entonces a Mario Garza, que llevaba 16 años en la organización y tenía experiencia en el desarrollo de jugadores, las operaciones en Latinoamérica y el desarrollo del béisbol, para que se encargara de los ojeadores internacionales en enero.
La transición tuvo un coste inmediato. Wandy Asigen, uno de los mejores jugadores de la promoción internacional de 2026, se echó atrás en el acuerdo que tenía previsto con los Yankees tras la marcha de Rowland y fichó por los Mets por 3,9 millones de dólares. Nueva York también empezó el periodo de fichajes con un fondo de 5,44 millones de dólares, el más bajo de la MLB (empatado con otro equipo) tras perder un millón de dólares por fichar a Max Fried.
Cuando Garza se hizo cargo, Brian Cashman describió algo que iba más allá de un simple cambio de personal.
«Es un gran evaluador de talento», dijo Cashman. «Conoce nuestros sistemas. Ya sabe todo el personal que queremos tener. Quieres evaluación, quieres que todo esté conectado con la ciencia del rendimiento y el análisis de datos. Eso le dará ventaja a la hora de relanzar ese departamento y seguir adelante».
Esas declaraciones públicas cobran ahora importancia porque dejaron claro, meses antes de septiembre, que Nueva York veía el departamento como algo que había que reconstruir, en lugar de simplemente mantener.
El relanzamiento se ha convertido en una reestructuración más amplia de los Yankees
Ese relanzamiento se ha acelerado.
Cinco empleados del departamento de ojeadores internacionales de los Yankees no han sido renovados en lo que el periodista Francys Romero ha descrito como una «primera oleada». Se trata de los ojeadores de la zona de la República Dominicana José Sabino y Arturo Peña Jr., el ojeador de la zona de Santo Domingo Moisés Brito, el asistente de vídeo Miguel Mojica y el supervisor de Venezuela José Gavidia.
Romero describió los cambios como parte de un plan más amplio.
«Los Yankees tienen previsto reestructurar su departamento de ojeadores internacionales y, según fuentes del sector, ya han despedido a cinco personas en los últimos días. Entre los ojeadores que no seguirán están José Sabino y Arturo Peña Jr. (ojeador de la zona de Cibao, República Dominicana), Moisés Brito (ojeador de la zona de Santo Domingo), Miguel Mojica (asistente de vídeo) y José Gavidia (supervisor de Venezuela)».
Estas medidas se produjeron tras la salida del veterano ojeador Víctor Mata, cuya trayectoria en los Yankees se prolongó durante más de tres décadas. Mata ayudó a evaluar o fichar a Canó, Sánchez, Soriano, Nova y Zoilo Almonte.
La naturaleza exacta de la salida de Mata sigue siendo objeto de debate. Romero informó de que los Yankees lo dejaron marchar. El periodista Mike Rodríguez ofreció una versión diferente, afirmando que Mata se retiró y recibió las prestaciones asociadas a su larga trayectoria en el equipo. Los Yankees no han dado públicamente una explicación detallada.
La cronología apunta a un reinicio planificado
La racha es más larga que los movimientos de esta semana.
A Rowland no le renovaron el contrato en noviembre. Garza fue nombrado en enero y Cashman utilizó públicamente la palabra «relanzamiento». Los Yankees funcionaron entonces toda la temporada bajo un nuevo liderazgo antes de la marcha de Mata y los cinco cambios adicionales en la plantilla que se produjeron en septiembre.
Esto apunta más bien a un reajuste estructural que a una reacción ante un solo prospecto o una sola promoción de fichajes.
Había motivos para replantearse los resultados. Un análisis de FanGraphs sobre el sistema de cantera de los Yankees, publicado en marzo, señalaba que el club solía destinar una gran parte de su fondo de bonificaciones internacionales a uno o dos jugadores caros y que demasiadas de esas apuestas millonarias no habían dado los frutos esperados.
En ese mismo informe se decía que el sistema necesitaba más talento entre los jugadores de campo tras las últimas salidas por graduación. Eso no aclara por qué se despidió a ningún ojeador, pero ayuda a entender por qué los Yankees se replantearían cómo identifican, valoran y forman a los jugadores internacionales.
La marcha de Asigen hizo que el tema cobrara más relevancia. Este campocorto de 16 años estaba considerado uno de los mejores jugadores de su generación y se esperaba que firmara con los Yankees, pero cambió de planes tras la salida de Rowland.
Ahora los comentarios que hizo Cashman en enero parecen más importantes
La pista más clara sobre qué hay detrás de la reorganización de los Yankees podría haber llegado ocho meses antes de los últimos cambios.
La descripción que hizo Cashman de Garza hacía hincapié en la colaboración entre la evaluación, la ciencia del rendimiento y el análisis de datos. El currículum de Garza une todas esas áreas. Antes de este puesto, fue director de desarrollo de béisbol en 2024 y 2025, y anteriormente trabajó en operaciones en Latinoamérica y en el desarrollo de jugadores internacionales.
Esto hace que los cambios parezcan menos un rechazo al ojeo tradicional y más un intento de cambiar cómo circula la información de ojeo por la organización.
El ojeo internacional sigue dependiendo de las relaciones, la evaluación presencial y el conocimiento local. La carrera de Mata puso de manifiesto ese valor. Pero ahora los Yankees están colocando al frente del departamento a un líder con experiencia reciente en desarrollo y sistemas.
La apuesta es importante. Nueva York está dejando atrás a miembros del equipo con profundas raíces en Latinoamérica, al tiempo que pide a un nuevo grupo que mantenga esas relaciones y modernice la evaluación al mismo tiempo.
El veredicto tardará años en salir
No hay resultados inmediatos que reflejen una reforma en el sistema de ojeadores internacionales.
Un cambio en la alineación se puede valorar esa misma noche. Pero una decisión que afecte a un joven promesa de 16 años puede que no dé frutos en las Grandes Ligas hasta dentro de cinco o seis años.
Eso es lo que hace que el momento sea tan significativo. Los Yankees tienen un balance de 88-63, se han asegurado un puesto en octubre y ocupan la primera plaza de comodín de la Liga Americana. Sin embargo, estos cambios están pensados para las plantillas mucho más allá de la actual carrera por los playoffs.
La cronología que se conoce está clara: Rowland se va, ascienden a Garza, se pierde a uno de los mejores fichajes, Mata se marcha y no se renueva a otros cinco miembros del personal internacional. Lo que los Yankees no han dicho públicamente es si habrá más cambios.
Por ahora, las declaraciones de Cashman en enero son las que ofrecen una explicación más clara. Los Yankees querían relanzar el departamento y vincular más estrechamente el trabajo de ojeadores con la ciencia del rendimiento y el análisis de datos.
Ocho meses después, ese relanzamiento está cambiando el perfil de las personas que decidirán qué jóvenes jugadores entrarán próximamente en el sistema de los Yankees.
¿Qué te parece? Deja tu comentario más abajo.

item.title: [Sports Illustrated] John Schreiber Experiment Is Paying Huge Dividends at Backend of Bullpen
